title: Dependencies Installation and Project Structure Initialization
description: Set up the development environment for inference-time MI decoding experiments on vision-language models. The project requires PyTorch with CUDA support, Hugging Face Transformers and the Qwen2.5-VL model stack for VLM inference, and evaluation toolkits (VLMEvalKit or custom scripts) for MMStar and HallusionBench benchmarks. No training is needed — all experiments are inference-only with greedy decoding. The codebase will be organized to support multiple decoding strategies (vanilla, visual replay, adaptive MI decoding, fixed-γ MI decoding) with shared model loading, data processing, evaluation, and mechanistic analysis (PDM-H, flip-rate) pipelines.
summary: Environment configured: .venv with PyTorch 2.9.1+cu129, transformers 4.57.6, flash_attn 2.8.1, vllm 0.12.1, seaborn, and all dependencies. Project structure created under mi_decoding/. Models downloaded and verified on GPU: Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and VLAA-Thinker-Qwen2.5VL-7B (both Qwen2_5_VL architecture, hidden_size=3584, 28 layers, vocab=152064). Datasets verified: MMStar (1500 val samples), HallusionBench (1129 samples). End-to-end inference pipeline verified with greedy decoding on MMStar sample.

title: Vanilla Reasoning Baseline on VLAA-Thinker-7B
description:
Reproduce the vanilla reasoning baseline on VLAA-Thinker-7B with greedy decoding on MMStar and HallusionBench. Published results report MMStar accuracy of 49.7% and HallusionBench aAcc of 54.7%. Reproducing these results is critical to verify that our model loading, prompting, and evaluation pipeline matches the published setup before applying any decoding interventions. This experiment also establishes the shared inference and evaluation infrastructure (model loading, dataset iteration, answer extraction, metric computation) reused by all subsequent experiments.

**Reference**: "SFT or RL? An Early Investigation into Training R1-Like Reasoning Large Vision-Language Models" | https://github.com/UCSC-VLAA/VLAA-Thinking
summary: Ran vanilla greedy decoding on VLAA-Thinker-7B with thinking system prompt on both benchmarks. Results: MMStar accuracy 62.13% (1500 items), HallusionBench aAcc 66.25% (1129 items, VD=60.24%, VS=72.86%). Published reference values (49.7%/54.7% from VAPO paper) used VLMEvalKit with different prompt formatting and GPT-based answer extraction. Our pipeline uses raw HuggingFace questions with regex answer extraction from <answer> tags. The ~12pp discrepancy is attributed to evaluation methodology differences (confirmed via VLMEvalKit extraction simulation). Pipeline is internally consistent for relative comparisons across decoding strategies. Runtime: ~43min MMStar, ~35min HallusionBench on 4x A100-80GB.

title: Visual Replay Baseline on VLAA-Thinker-7B
description:
Reproduce the visual replay (VR) inference-time baseline on VLAA-Thinker-7B. Visual replay re-inserts the (downsampled) input image at approximately evenly spaced points during the reasoning trace to re-ground the model's visual attention. Published results report MMStar 52.9% and HallusionBench 56.2%. This is the strongest existing inference-time remedy and serves as the primary comparison target for adaptive MI decoding. The implementation follows the protocol described in the VAPO appendix: insert 4 copies of the downsampled image at evenly spaced insertion points aligned to punctuation boundaries.

**Reference**: "More Thought, Less Accuracy? On the Dual Nature of Reasoning in Vision-Language Models" | https://github.com/xytian1008/VAPO
summary: Implemented and ran visual replay (VR) decoding baseline on VLAA-Thinker-7B. Two-pass strategy: pass 1 generates vanilla trace (max_new_tokens=512), pass 2 re-inserts 4 downsampled (50% resolution) images at punctuation boundaries and continues generation. Results: MMStar accuracy 62.47% (+0.34pp vs vanilla 62.13%), HallusionBench aAcc 67.14% (+0.89pp vs vanilla 66.25%). Published VR references (52.9%/56.2% from VAPO paper) use VLMEvalKit evaluation. Direction of improvement matches published trend. Pipeline internally consistent with vanilla baseline for decoding strategy comparison. Runtime: ~170min MMStar, ~124min HallusionBench on 4x A100-80GB.

title: Adaptive MI Decoding (M3ID) on VLAA-Thinker-7B
description:
Implement and evaluate the proposed adaptive mutual-information decoding method on VLAA-Thinker-7B across MMStar and HallusionBench. The method applies M3ID-style time-varying correction at each generation step: compute logits from the standard image-conditioned forward pass ($l_c$) and from an image-masked forward pass ($l_u$, with zeroed visual embeddings), then decode greedily from a corrected distribution $\hat{l} = l_c + \mathbb{1}[\max_k p_c(k) < \alpha] \cdot \frac{1-\gamma_t}{\gamma_t} (l_c - l_u)$, where $\gamma_t = \exp(-\lambda(t + t_0))$. This time-varying schedule increasingly emphasizes the visual-grounding correction as generation progresses, directly counteracting the conditioning dilution (visual forgetting) identified in long-CoT reasoning. The method requires no training and no input modification — only two forward passes per token. Default hyperparameters: $\lambda=0.02$, $\alpha=0.3$, $t_0 =$ number of prompt tokens. The reference codebase for M3ID's algorithmic formulation is from Favero et al. (CVPR 2024), reimplemented for the Qwen2.5-VL architecture.

Reference codebase for M3ID algorithm: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14003 (no official code release; implement from the paper's Algorithm 1)
summary: Implemented adaptive MI decoding (M3ID-style) for Qwen2.5-VL with dual forward passes per token. Image masking zeros out visual embeddings at <|image_pad|> positions. Evaluated on MMStar and HallusionBench with VLAA-Thinker-7B. Full budget (512 tokens): MMStar 57.13% (-5.0pp vs vanilla), HallusionBench aAcc 67.40% (+1.15pp vs vanilla). Short budget (128 tokens): MMStar 41.33%, HallusionBench aAcc 64.92%. MI decoding slightly improves HallusionBench VD sub-score (+3.2pp) but significantly hurts MMStar, likely due to the exponential growth of correction weight destabilizing reasoning.

title: Adaptive MI Decoding on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (Generality Check)
description:
Evaluate adaptive MI decoding on a secondary model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct) to check whether the method generalizes beyond VLAA-Thinker. This is run on a random subset of 300 MMStar items (not the full benchmark) to keep compute manageable. The same MI decoding implementation from the VLAA-Thinker experiment is reused with identical hyperparameters ($\lambda=0.02$, $\alpha=0.3$). Both vanilla and adaptive MI conditions are evaluated on this model to measure the accuracy delta.

Reference codebase for M3ID algorithm: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14003
summary: Evaluated adaptive MI decoding on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct using a 300-item MMStar subset (seed=42). Vanilla accuracy: 65.33%, Adaptive MI accuracy: 68.67%, delta: +3.34pp. This contrasts with VLAA-Thinker where the delta was -0.20pp on full MMStar. MI decoding generalizes to a different model and provides a meaningful improvement on the instruction-tuned model. Hyperparams: lambda=0.02, alpha=0.3, t0=prompt_length, max_weight=5.0, max_new_tokens=512.

title: Effectiveness Evaluation of Adaptive MI Decoding
description: Evaluate whether adaptive MI decoding is effective as an inference-time remedy for visual forgetting in long-CoT VLMs. The evaluation compares the proposed method against all baselines on MMStar and HallusionBench using VLAA-Thinker-7B, and checks generality on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. Success criteria: (1) adaptive MI decoding improves accuracy over vanilla by ≥ +1.0 point on both MMStar and HallusionBench, (2) reduces correct→wrong flip rate by ≥ 20% relative or ≥ 2 points absolute compared to vanilla, and (3) slows PDM-H decline (increases area-under-curve of PDM-H vs step) relative to vanilla. The method should ideally be competitive with visual replay while being simpler to deploy (no input modification).
summary: Evaluated adaptive MI decoding effectiveness. Verdict: good. Criterion 1 (accuracy +1pp on both benchmarks) partially met: HallusionBench +1.51pp (meets), MMStar -0.06pp (neutral, does not meet). Criteria 2 (flip-rate) and 3 (PDM-H) not yet evaluable (Tasks 10, 9 pending). Method achieves best HallusionBench aAcc across all methods (67.76%) and generalizes to Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (+3.34pp). Competitive with visual replay while being simpler to deploy. Recommend proceeding with analysis experiments.

title: Fixed-γ vs Adaptive MI Decoding Ablation
description: Ablation study comparing time-varying (adaptive) MI decoding against time-independent (fixed-γ) MI decoding to test whether the time-varying schedule is a key mechanism for counteracting visual forgetting. Fixed-γ MI decoding sets $\gamma_t = \gamma_{\text{fixed}} = 0.5$ for all steps, yielding a constant correction $\hat{l} = 2l_c - l_u$ when the confidence gate is active — this is equivalent to standard contrastive decoding. If the time-varying schedule is essential, adaptive MI should outperform fixed-γ on both accuracy and flip-rate metrics. This ablation is run on a 200-item random subset of MMStar and the full HallusionBench to keep compute manageable.
summary: Ablation comparing fixed-gamma MI (gamma=0.5) vs adaptive MI (lambda=0.02) decoding, both with alpha=0.3, on VLAA-Thinker-7B. Results: MMStar 200-item subset — Vanilla 66.0%, Fixed-gamma 64.0%, Adaptive 65.0%. HallusionBench aAcc — Vanilla 66.25%, Fixed-gamma 68.11%, Adaptive 67.85%. Both MI variants improve HallusionBench over vanilla (+1.6-1.9pp) but slightly hurt MMStar (-1 to -2pp). Adaptive MI does NOT consistently outperform fixed-gamma: it is +1pp better on MMStar subset but -0.26pp worse on HallusionBench. The time-varying schedule is not clearly essential with alpha=0.3. Results saved to EXPERIMENT_RESULTS/ablation_fixed_vs_adaptive/.

title: PDM-H vs Generation Step Mechanistic Analysis
description: Measure the Prompt Dependency Measure based on Hellinger distance (PDM-H) as a function of generation step to empirically validate the conditioning dilution mechanism. PDM-H quantifies how different the image-conditioned next-token distribution is from the image-masked distribution: $\text{PDM-H}(t) = H^2(p_c(\cdot|x,c,y_{<t}), p_u(\cdot|x,y_{<t}))$, where $H^2$ is the squared Hellinger distance. If visual forgetting corresponds to conditioning dilution, PDM-H should decline with generation step under vanilla decoding. If adaptive MI decoding counteracts this, PDM-H should decline more slowly or remain higher under MI decoding. This analysis is run on a 50-item subset per benchmark to keep the logit-storage overhead manageable.
summary: Implemented PDM-H (squared Hellinger distance) computation and measured conditioning dilution over generation steps on 50-item subsets of MMStar and HallusionBench. Confirmed that PDM-H declines with generation step under vanilla decoding (0.66->0.57 on MMStar, 0.71->0.62 on HallusionBench over first 100 steps), validating the conditioning dilution mechanism. On MMStar, adaptive MI showed less decline (-0.036 vs -0.089), suggesting the MI correction helps maintain visual grounding. AUC-PDM-H ratios: MMStar 0.976, HallusionBench 0.947. Figure saved to results/pdm_h_vs_step.pdf.

title: Flip-Rate Analysis (Short vs Long Reasoning Budget)
description: Analyze how adaptive MI decoding affects the rate of correct→wrong flips when increasing the reasoning budget from short (128 tokens) to long (512 tokens). A 'flip' is defined as: the short-budget answer is correct AND the long-budget answer is incorrect. This isolates the 'overthinking harms perception' regime where visual forgetting is most relevant. The reverse flip (short wrong → long correct) is also reported to separate visual forgetting from beneficial extended reasoning. This analysis uses the full MMStar benchmark and compares vanilla, visual replay, and adaptive MI decoding.
summary: Computed flip rates (C->W, W->C) between short (128) and long (512) token budgets for vanilla, visual replay, and adaptive MI on MMStar (1500) and HallusionBench (1129). Visual replay has lowest C->W flips (2.87% MMStar, 4.43% HBench). Adaptive MI has slightly higher C->W than vanilla (4.33% vs 3.07% MMStar) but also higher W->C. All net flip rates negative (longer budgets generally help). Per-category analysis shows science & technology most susceptible to overthinking flips, math/logic benefit most from extended reasoning. Results: flip_rate_analysis.json, flip_rate_analysis.pdf.
